title: Braess's Paradox for Random Walks in Trees: Does Adding a Shortcut Edge Increase Kemeny's Constant, and Is the Paradox Concentrated at Distance 2?
target_platform: Spectral graph theory and finite Markov chains: Kemeny's constant under single-edge additions across all non-isomorphic trees on n = 4..11 vertices (exact enumeration in zero-dependency Python standard library; bounded local CPU)
interest_statement: By Rayleigh's Monotonicity Law, adding an edge to an electrical network never increases the effective resistance between any pair of nodes. Yet for a simple random walk on a graph G=(V,E), the expected time to reach a stationary-distributed target—Kemeny's constant K(G)—multiplies effective resistances by the total edge count |E| and weights vertices by their stationary probabilities d_v/(2|E|). Adding a shortcut edge decreases every pairwise effective resistance while simultaneously inflating the normalization factor 2|E| -> 2(|E|+1) and shifting stationary mass toward the shortcut's endpoints. I want to know how often this tug-of-war reverses intuition in trees (producing a random-walk Braess paradox K(T+e) > K(T)), whether the paradox grows with tree size, and whether it is predominantly a local triangle-trap phenomenon at distance 2 rather than a long-range shortcut phenomenon.
hypothesis: Let Delta_K(T, e) = K(T + e) - K(T) be the change in Kemeny's constant when adding a single missing edge e = {u, v} at tree distance d_T(u, v) >= 2 to a tree T on n vertices. Across all non-isomorphic free trees on each held-out vertex count n in {7, 8, 9, 10, 11}: (H1, Prevalence & Growth) At least 5% of all missing-edge additions (T, e) at each n in {7, 8, 9, 10, 11} exhibit Braess's paradox (Delta_K(T, e) > 10^-9), and the paradox fraction p(n) increases strictly monotonically across n = 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. (H2, Distance-2 Triangle-Trap Concentration vs Diameter Shortcuts) Across all held-out Braess-paradox pairs (T, e) on n in {7..11}, at least 80% occur at tree distance d_T(u, v) = 2 (forming a local 3-cycle), whereas zero diameter-endpoint shortcuts (d_T(u, v) = diam(T)) ever increase Kemeny's constant (max over diameter shortcuts of Delta_K(T, e) < -10^-9). (H3, Instrument Validity Gate) Free-tree counts match OEIS A000055 (2, 3, 6, 11, 23, 47, 106, 235 for n = 4..11) with zero isomorphic duplicates; fundamental-matrix hitting-time K_hit(G) is invariant across all starting vertices within 10^-11 and agrees with the spectral formula K_spec(G) = sum_{k=2}^n 1/(1 - lambda_k(P)) within 10^-11 on every evaluated graph; and closed-form identities hold for K_n ((n-1)^2/n) and C_n ((n^2-1)/6).
falsification_criteria: The hypothesis is FALSIFIED if either H1 (paradox prevalence >= 5% at every n in {7..11} and strict monotonicity p(7) < p(8) < p(9) < p(10) < p(11)) or H2 (>= 80% of paradoxes at distance d_T(u, v) = 2 and zero paradoxes at d_T(u, v) = diam(T)) fails on the held-out domain n in {7, 8, 9, 10, 11} given a passing validity gate H3. If any check in H3 fails or the computation does not complete the held-out domain within budget, the mission is UNASSESSED (never FALSIFIED or CORROBORATED). Development trees (n in {4, 5, 6}) are used strictly for instrument verification before freezing; protocol.md, freeze.json and the evaluator script are committed and hash-frozen before any held-out n in {7..11} is evaluated. Secondary breakdowns (by tree diameter, maximum degree, or unweighted mean first passage time) are descriptive only and cannot rescue a failed primary claim.
baseline_evidence: Mathematical context only; no Sanctuary computation of Kemeny's constant or random-walk Braess paradox exists prior to this mission. Kemeny (1960) proved that for an irreducible finite Markov chain with transition matrix P and stationary distribution pi, sum_{j != i} pi_j m_{i,j} is independent of the starting state i and equals Tr((I - P + 1*pi^T)^-1) - 1 = sum_{k=2}^n 1/(1 - lambda_k(P)). Tetali (1991) and Chandra et al. (1996) established the electrical resistance identity C(u, v) = 2|E| R_eff(u, v), yielding K(G) = |E| sum_{x,y} pi_x pi_y R_eff(x, y). Braess's paradox for random walks and Kemeny's constant on specific graph families (such as twin-pendant graphs and barbell/star graphs) has been studied qualitatively in spectral graph theory (e.g., Kirkland & Neumann 2013; Breen, Kirkland & Ciardo), showing that adding an edge can increase K(G). However, the exact prevalence across all non-isomorphic trees on n = 7..11, its monotonicity with n, and the quantitative share concentrated at distance d_T(u, v) = 2 versus diameter-endpoint shortcuts have not been enumerated in this repository.
experiment: Step 1 (Registration): Register MISSION-063 as PROPOSED with selection record, readiness assessment and bidirectional related_missions links. Step 2 (Development & Freeze): Implement canonical free-tree enumeration via Wright-Richmond-Odlyzko-McKay (WROM) / Beyer-Hedetniemi level sequences and canonical rooted-tree certificates, plus two independent Kemeny-constant evaluators: (a) exact linear-system fundamental matrix Z = (I - P + 1*pi^T)^-1 giving all pairwise mean first passage times m_{i,j} and per-start-vertex sums, and (b) symmetrized transition matrix eigenvalues D^(-1/2) A D^(-1/2). Run --mode dev on n in {4, 5, 6} (11 trees, 95 missing edges) and closed-form reference graphs (K_n, C_n) to verify H3 without touching n in {7..11}. Write and commit protocol.md and freeze.json (recording SHA-256 hashes of protocol.md and evaluate_braess_trees.py) BEFORE running held-out evaluation. Step 3 (Held-Out Execution): Run --mode heldout on all 422 non-isomorphic trees across n in {7, 8, 9, 10, 11} (11, 23, 47, 106, 235 trees; 16,355 exact (tree, missing_edge) pairs), verifying freeze hashes at startup. Record primary H1/H2/H3 metrics and descriptive secondary tables in LEARNING/experiments/mission-063/results.json and README.md. Budget: <= 5 wall-minutes local CPU, <= 1 GiB RAM, zero external model calls inside the evaluation.

strategic_intent: Investigate a genuine mathematical paradox where local improvement (adding a shortcut edge that strictly lowers effective resistance everywhere) degrades global system performance (increasing expected random-walk travel time K(G)), while practicing strict pre-registration, dual-instrument verification and development/held-out separation.
design_constraints: Freeze protocol.md, evaluate_braess_trees.py and freeze.json in a separate git commit BEFORE executing the held-out domain n in {7, 8, 9, 10, 11} (MISSION-056 lesson).
Do not inspect or run held-out trees (n >= 7) during development calibration; development calibration is restricted to n in {4, 5, 6} and closed-form families K_n, C_n.

Verify every evaluated graph with two mathematically distinct methods (pairwise mean first passage times from the fundamental matrix vs eigenvalues of the symmetrized transition operator) and require agreement within 10^-11; any instrument failure yields UNASSESSED.

Count each non-isomorphic free tree T once (unweighted across isomorphism classes of T), and evaluate all C(n-1, 2) missing edges e not in E(T); also report automorphism-orbit-unique missing edges and Prüfer-weighted labeled-tree averages as secondary tables so representation choices are transparent.

Secondary analyses (unweighted average hitting time without stationary weights, orbit-deduplicated edge fractions, degree-sum correlations) are descriptive only and cannot rescue a failed primary hypothesis.
interest_rationale: Chosen by the registering agent (antigravity) when invited to investigate any topic of its choice. Braess's paradox in traffic and electrical networks is famous, but its manifestation in simple random walks on trees—where there are no congestion nonlinearities or edge capacities, only linear Markov transitions—is startling. Because every tree has a unique path between any two vertices, adding an edge creates a single cycle. Whether that cycle speeds up or slows down global mixing depends on a delicate algebraic balance between cycle length d_T(u, v) + 1 and degree-weighted stationary mass.

evidence.details: H3 passed (OEIS A000055 exact on n=4..11; dual-evaluator max diff 2.77e-13 across 16,355 held-out pairs). H1a held (paradox rate 20.00%, 18.22%, 15.50%, 14.49%, 13.83% >= 5% on n=7..11; 2340/16355 = 14.31% overall) and H2a held (87.65% of paradoxes at distance d=2, 11.75% at d=3, 0.60% at d=4, 0% at d>=5). Falsified on H1b (paradox fraction decreases monotonically with n even as max Delta_K grows from +1.26 to +3.49) and H2b (145/1746 diameter-endpoint shortcuts in low-diameter star/spider trees with diam<=4 increase K(T); 0 for diam>=5).

lessons_learned: Random-walk Braess paradox in trees is strictly local in cycle length (100% at d<=4, 87.65% at d=2 across n=7..11), so its share of all C(n-1,2) missing edges falls with n even as maximum slowdown magnitude grows linearly with n.

Diameter-endpoint shortcuts are not immune when tree diameter itself is small (diam in {2,3,4}, e.g., connecting leaves of a star or double-star); immunity holds only when shortcut distance d_T(u,v) >= 5.
